title: Reform promises to increase tax-free personal allowance to £15,000
description: Reform UK is promising to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000, if it wins the next general election. Robert Jenrick, the party's econo
body: Reform UK is promising to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000, if it wins the next general election. Robert Jenrick, the party's economic spokesman, has pledged to introduce the tax cut within the first 100 days if he became chancellor saying it would provide "money that people really need right now".It is seen by Reform insiders as the flagship policy announcement of its conference and perhaps their biggest tax policy between now and the general election.Asked about two senior Reform aides being investigated by the party following a Channel 4 News undercover broadcast into claims about funding, Jenrick told the BBC Nigel Farage had acted swiftly and they had been suspended. In undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totalled £500,000.Electoral law sets out that to be a donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.Farage said on Friday that his party had "done nothing wrong" and had taken "no illegal money. In fact no money was taken at all."Jukes denied wrongdoing and said he was stepping away from politics "in order to clear my name". Orr told Sky News he would cooperate fully with the party's internal investigation.Orr is an associate professor of Philosophy of Religion at Cambridge University's Faculty of Divinity.  Responding to the Channel 4 News and Verbatim report, Cambridge University said it was "looking into these matters".Jenrick told the Today programme that the party had taken legal advice and it did not believe it had done anything wrong.Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported the party to the Metropolitan Police.The Electoral Commission has said it is considering "all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit" and was in contact with the police.On tax measures, Reform estimates that increasing the tax-free threshold by £2,430 would save most taxpayers £500 a year and 2.9 million people would stop paying income tax altogether. It says the policy would cost £17.7bn in the first year, rising to £21bn by the fifth year and could be paid for through £80bn of public spending cuts the party plans to make. Jenrick told BBC Breakfast Reform would pay for the policy by "cutting out the waste".Reform has said its spending cuts would include a £50bn reduction in welfare spending.Half of the £353bn of welfare spending goes on the state pension, but Reform has said it will not cut this proportion.The bulk of the funding would come from reducing the cost of welfare, Jenrick said, by not paying benefits to people who are not British citizens and helping people who are off work due to their mental health back into jobs. Jenrick also said the UK would "stop paying foreign aid to rich countries", adding that "we should be looking after British people first"."Yes, we'll pay for disaster relief but the vast majority of that budget should be spent on the priorities of our own people," he said. Reform hopes to raise £10bn by scrapping net-zero programmes and Jenrick said, as the UK only amounted to 1% of the world's emissions, it was not sensible to be trying to decarbonise faster than other countries as that was "just impoverishing our own people".The party hopes to raise £8bn by reducing the number of civil servants and £7.1bn by capping the foreign aid budget.The policy is expected to be announced in Jenrick's conference speech later."As chancellor, I will wake each morning with one purpose. To make Britain a better place to be a worker than it was the day before," he is expected to say.He is expected to add: "1.3 million were dragged into paying tax last year alone. Why? Because the tax-free allowance has been stuck at 12 and a half grand since 2021. And Labour has frozen it until 2031. "That betrayal costs a full-time worker on the minimum wage more than £750 a year. And now for the first time, the freeze means they're going to be taxing the state pension. What a disgrace."In its manifesto before the general election in 2024, Reform said it wanted to lift the threshold to £20,000. Jenrick will tell conference activists this remains his long-term aim.The personal allowance threshold currently stands at £12,570. Anyone earning more than £100,000 starts to lose their personal allowance. For every £2 earned above the threshold the basic allowance decreases by £1.Shortly after becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham told the Times that the "frustration" of people in his Makerfield constituency about the frozen allowance had "lodged in my mind".He later said that "all of this would be looked at" in the upcoming Budget but that any change would be "difficult given the financial circumstances".

schema.headline: Reform promises to increase tax-free personal allowance to £15,000

title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
description: That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course,
body: That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course, given that President Reagan provided material support to Margaret Thatcher during the Falklands War in 1982  – an act which reinforced the long-standing alliance between London and Washington in times of conflict.For Trump, however, that mutual support – the "Special Relationship" – was eroded by Sir Keir Starmer when the UK Government chose not to join the US war on Iran."You weren't there to help me", the president retorted in an interview with GB News this week. The Falklands were "a long way away", he said. The Falkland Islanders – who voted almost unanimously to remain a British overseas territory in 2013 – would point out that distance from London to the Falklands is fractionally shorter than the distance between Washington DC and the US territory of Guam, in the western Pacific.Still, Trump's words have undoubtedly galvanised Milei. As have the opinion polls. He urgently needs a boost ahead of a presidential election next year in which one of his challengers, his former vice-president, Victoria Villarruel, has presented herself as a tougher defender of national sovereignty and attacked Milei's diplomatic approach on the Falklands as failing.Domestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it.With two energy companies – the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK – due to undertake work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added.On Saturday morning Milei's office said on X that it was launching sanctions proceedings against 45 people and companies. The announcement did not identify those targeted and it is not yet clear what impact they will have.In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally. The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the "Don-roe Doctrine", a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas.Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics.Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship".

schema.headline: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder

title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
description: A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before collidin
body: A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news."No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra £2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra £20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.It also ranks highest for burglary, sexual offences, violence with injury, and criminal damage and arson.Fuller said Cleveland Police had also experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force."It absolutely needs to change," she said. Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."Recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues."We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fuelling organised crime."When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said. "They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."The five who died in the Volkswagen on 22 August were aged between 17 and 23. Four of them had previous convictions, including for assaulting police officers and theft, Cleveland Police previously said.Since the crash, the force has responded to at least two incidents it believes are in retaliation for the crash.It has also had to grapple with a house fire in Middlesbrough that killed a woman and her niece, and left several others injured, which police could not rule out was linked to organised crime.A 23-year-old man has been charged with murder in relation to the deaths of Natalie McDonald, 34, and Valentina Foster, seven.Fuller also paid tribute to the two officers who died in the A66 crash - PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough."My heart goes out to their families - it really does," she said. "My grief can't compare to theirs, nor to the officers and staff who've worked closely with Matty and Tom for a long time."The Home Office said it was grateful to Cleveland Police for delivering a robust response in difficult circumstances. A spokesperson said: "We have been in regular contact with Cleveland Police and local leaders, ensuring they have the support they need and engaging on their financial concerns."This additional £2m targeted funding will help Cleveland Police tackle serious crime. Beyond this, the force will receive up to £197.8m in funding in the 2026/2027 financial year - a 3.7% uplift in cash."We have also committed to a wider review of the police funding formula to ensure that force funding is fair and responsive to local needs."

schema.headline: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding

title: Lindsay Clancy murder trial has divided US on whether she's victim or criminal
description: Figure caption, Inside court as judge declares a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy caseByAna FaguyReporting fromreporting from court in MassachusettsBrandon
body: Figure caption, Inside court as judge declares a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy caseByAna FaguyReporting fromreporting from court in MassachusettsBrandon Drenon and Sheila FlynnUpdated 1 hour agoWarning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicideJodi Fournier spent 15 days at the courthouse - sitting, listening and waiting. It was a personal duty, she felt, to show support for Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother charged with murdering her three children.Katelyn Kazmirci, from North Carolina, convinced her mother to make a detour to the courthouse in Plymouth on their way to a family funeral, intrigued by the case she had followed on TikTok.All around them, dozens of women wearing pink rallied in support of Clancy. Not everyone felt the same and across the country, on social media and at dinner tables, Americans have been debating the case with passion.For nearly seven weeks, the trial transfixed and divided the nation on whether Clancy was a victim or a criminal who deserved to be behind bars.The 36-year-old nurse's defence team argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis when she strangled her young children and so could not be held criminally responsible. The prosecution alleged the killings were intentional and calculated.The judge declared a mistrial on Friday after jurors - who had heard the testimony of dozens of witnesses and deliberated for 40 hours - failed to come to a uninanimous decision.Their inability to agree mirrored the wider discourse around the trial - one that trial attendee Maryanne Drysdale, 65, saw play out within her own family.She and her 28-year-old daughter believe Clancy needs mental health treatment, not prison, while her three adult sons, who have children of similar age to Clancy's, completely disagree."It's black and white for them, [Clancy] killed the kids and that's that," she said. "I brought these kids up - how can we think so differently about this?"Image caption, Jodi Fournier spent more than two weeks outside the courthouse to show support for ClancyFournier believes Clancy was wronged by the US health system and felt compelled, as a woman and a mother, to show up for a case that has given a spotlight to postpartum struggles."It only takes one person to change the narrative," she said. "This is a global issue. This isn't just Massachusetts-small-town. This is... women everywhere."Clancy claims she experienced hallucinations and delusions before strangling her three children - five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months old - and then jumping from a second-floor window, leaving her paralysed.The court heard testimony from more than 10 expert witnesses on Clancy's mental and postpartum health during the trial.But some of them seemed to dispute the defence's claim that postpartum psychosis  - a rare post-childbirth condition characterised by mania and depression - precluded Clancy from criminal liability.Jennifer Tufts, who treated Clancy during more than a dozen sessions over five months, testified that she had not shown signs of psychosis. Psychiatrist Avram Mack later testified that the American Psychiatric Association did not recognise postpartum psychosis as a diagnosis. These declarations only deepened staunch opinions for many - on both sides.Texas mother-of-four Nicole Russell, who followed the trial remotely, noted the prosecution's presentation of how much medical care and support Clancy had received - from doctors, her husband, nanny and family - calling it "way more help" than most mothers receive.Clancy's struggles were said to have begun following the birth of her youngest child. She repeatedly sought care, visiting a hospital emergency room, different medical professionals and even calling a suicide hotline.Many observers took that as evidence that Clancy had been proactive and done everything within her power to heal but had been failed by the system, prompting sympathy from some.Image caption, Melissa Merrill says she, like Clancy, suffered suicidal ideation after giving birth Melissa Merrill had been treated at the same hospital as Clancy after the birth of her son."I see myself in her, as a mum who had suicidal ideation," she told the BBC outside the Plymouth courthouse.Throughout the weeks of emotional testimony, Clancy, who uses a wheelchair, could be seen crying, holding her attorney's hand and making agonised utterances in court as sometimes harrowing details were shared. After one of the trial days, Merrill rushed to Clancy's defence attorney outside the court and gave him a pink envelope holding a message of support and hope for his client, believing Clancy was a "sad, defeated woman".But other parents, like Texas mother Russell, railed against "toxic empathy", insisting Clancy was "not a martyr or a symbol for tired mums"."Lindsay Clancy cannot be the poster child of what difficult motherhood looks like, because millions of mothers give birth to children and endure all kinds of hardship, and they do not hurt their children," Russell argued.Figure caption, The moment judge declares a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy caseThe discourse around the Clancy trial was prominent on social media, with many users being hard-pressed to find a platform where the case was not being mentioned, if not being subject to myriad conspiracy theories.Clancy's mother, sister and former husband all testified to her deteriorating mental state in the run-up to the murders, but her ex Patrick Clancy was singled out online for wild vitriol and cover-up accusations.There were claims that he was to blame for the murders, despite his wife never denying killing their children, nor that she had been the only adult at home at the time. This thrust him into the limelight, with tabloids snapping photos of him travelling and with his new wife. His lawyers issued a statement to CNN in August calling the facts "indisputable"."Patrick Clancy has suffered an unspeakable and unimaginable loss," they said. "Unfortunately, the tragedy Patrick has experienced has been compounded by patently false, defamatory and injurious public statements."Image source, The Boston Globe via Getty ImagesImage caption, Clancy supporters - many wearing pink - huddled outside the courthouseImage source, The Boston Globe via Getty ImagesImage caption, Those who believed Clancy should be held accountable for the killings also had a presence outside the court The case became a flashpoint for gender discussion, too, with opinions often divided along gender lines.Father-of-three Vincenzo Vazquez, who followed the trial from Illinois, believes gender has a lot to do with Clancy's treatment, doubting that the public would show similar sympathy if a father were on trial for the same charges."Whatever someone is dealing with, I don't think there's ever an appropriate time or an excuse or a justification to, you know, kill children of your own, or kill any children," he said. He said he felt "very sad and a little disgusted to see how many people are rallying behind her", adding: "I think people should be out there rallying for justice for the children. They're three beautiful kids that had a future in front of them."The decision to declare a mistrial after seven days of deadlocked jury deliberations has left the status of the case - and Clancy's future - unclear. A hearing at the end of the month could establish whether prosecutors will move ahead with second trial or attempt to reach a plea deal. For now, the debates elsewhere will no doubt continue.If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

schema.headline: Lindsay Clancy murder trial has divided US on whether she's victim or criminal

title: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
description: Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined. These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see co-ordinate
body: Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined. These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see co-ordinated vandalism. Yet here, four surveillance cameras were attacked and cut down in the middle of the night.The metal poles were severed, leaving the distinctive black oval cameras and accompanying solar panels lying on the ground. On some of the cameras was a red sign reading: "Notice. 24/7 video recording."These cameras are run by a company called Flock Safety and this sabotage, which happened in late July, is a signal of growing concern over the nationwide spread of sophisticated AI-powered surveillance systems. Similar vandalism incidents have occurred in Minnesota, California and Georgia.Proponents say they have made communities safer and have helped dramatically increase the rate at which crimes are solved. But recent examples of misuse have caused concern. Critics say the cameras, which take pictures of the rear of every car that drives past, are overly broad investigative tools that treat civilians like suspects.They see the little black poles popping up in their neighbourhoods as visible reminders of state power, at a time when public confidence in institutions is historically low and many are concerned about the accelerating pace of technological change and the influence of AI on people's lives.Listen: ‘Big Surveillance’, Flock and ICEFounded in 2017, Flock Safety has become one of the country's biggest makers of Automatic Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs). These AI-powered cameras take a picture of the rear of every car that drives past. Footage is retained for a specified amount of time.But little is known about the extent to which Flock is being used - the company does not publish exact data, but says it works with more than 7,000 communities nationwide and estimates that there are approximately 100,000 cameras deployed.Records obtained by the BBC provide a rare glimpse into the extensive network of cameras and surveillance tech being used in America's fourth largest city, Houston, including the use of controversial facial recognition software powered by artificial intelligence.Flock is not just selling cameras - it is selling access to a database that can include thousands of cameras from around the country. Older ALPRs did not have this vast network, which is a major selling point for law enforcement.For example, Houston's Metro Transit Authority owns 35 cameras. But documents show Metro has access to around 20,000 devices in the Flock network - including some as far as Albany County, New York.And as Flock expands, so too can the scope of investigations. Documents released to the BBC show how the network has grown year-on-year. In the Cypress-Fairbanks independent school district, a typical licence plate lookup in April 2024 searched around 270 networks of cameras.By April 2025, the typical search scope had almost doubled to around 500 networks. In April 2026, 20% of searches were conducted across more than 6,000 networks.Critics in Houston say this national network concerns them more than individual cameras. Christopher Rivera, from the Texas Civil Rights Project, worries that authorities could use "these databases to search our everyday routines, which ultimately scrapes out our routes to work, where our children go to school, and where we worship - and that's very problematic".There have been recent incidents of privacy breaches that have caught national attention. Last week, a police officer in Kentucky was charged after using the Flock system to track his ex-girlfriend - who filed a protection order - over 2,000 times.He was caught using Flock's newly mandatory, AI-powered audit tool that flags suspicious use.Others are concerned about Flock being a way for police to avoid warrants, which are usually required to search a person's property or tap their phone. In 2025, a detective in Johnson County, Texas, searched over 80,000 images to locate a woman suspected of having an abortion. He did not have a warrant.CCTV cameras, licence-plate readers and surveillance are not new. But the scale of Flock's network and the integration of AI in modern surveillance tech is a recent development and it's turned Flock into a household name. Americans who otherwise ignored the cameras in their cities have started to notice and tune into the capabilities of the technology around them.With AI, unlike older licence-plate readers, law enforcement can search surveillance footage with a string of words like "Caucasian man, blue shirt" - not just a licence-plate image.One thing Flock does not use is facial recognition. But that does not mean police departments are avoiding that tech. Critics say it violates human rights, is susceptible to misidentifying innocent people, and can be biased against minorities.The BBC has received documents revealing that Harris County Sheriff's Office, which covers Houston, uses other facial recognition technology, Clearview AI. The tool includes a database of more than 70 billion images, many of which were scraped from public internet sources including social media. The documents, including purchase orders and a license agreement, show that the county's Clearview AI contract currently runs through to March 2027.Several European countries have issued the company with data protection fines, including a £7.5m penalty from the UK's Information Commissioner.Harris County Sheriff's Office use of this facial recognition technology has not been reported before. It did not respond to requests for comment.Police say surveillance technology like this, including Flock cameras, is important for fighting crime."It's a very good tool," says Chief Ray Schultz of the Memorial Villages Police Department - a small jurisdiction within Houston. "It makes the community safer." Before purchasing a Flock ALPR, his department would recover an average of three stolen cars a year. Now, this figure is 45, Schultz says.Some crimes solved in recent years would have been "impossible" without Flock, he adds. Last month, Schultz used the tool to find an elderly woman with dementia who had driven 60 miles from Galveston to Houston and had gotten lost. "We were able to find her and reunite her with her family."Schultz says that it is important for agencies to have strong policies governing ALPR use and officers that misuse the system should be held accountable."But don't throw out a tool that is valuable, that can help recover a missing child."Jasmine Khadem Gonzalez, an immigrant rights organiser, is worried that law enforcement might "use [the Flock] database to tell ICE where somebody is".The federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency does not have a contract with Flock directly. However, there have been reports of police officers citing "immigration" or "ice" as a reason for searching for a licence plate.Jessie, an immigrant from Central America, noticed a Flock camera outside her house last month. She asked the BBC to not use her real name out of fear it could impact a pending case to extend her green card."It makes me feel as if I'm being stalked," she says.In response, she's changed her commute to work. "I try to take different routes every day so there's not a pattern."But whether individual law enforcement agencies share info with the federal government is unclear. Federal immigration enforcement cannot access Flock data directly, Flock's CEO says. But some police departments have standing agreements with federal immigration enforcement to work together.In Harris County, a proposed Flock contract amendment initially included the explicit authorisation to share camera data with federal law enforcement, but this provision was later removed after push-back from campaigners.Some jurisdictions have opted not to renew contracts with Flock as a result of these concerns, including large metropolitan areas like Los Angeles, Seattle and Austin.In total, more than 200 communities have cancelled or not renewed their contracts since 2021 - including 90 in August alone - according to advocacy group Secure Justice, external. Their reasons for cancelling may include cost and concerns about data privacy. Nationally, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have suggested that there ought to be guardrails and several candidates have made it a campaign issue for the upcoming midterms. Republican Congressman Keith Self has proposed legislation that would require federal agencies to get warrants before accessing Flock data.The company itself has also amended some of its policies, such as requiring mandatory audits and reducing the default period that data stays on a server from 30 days to seven, unless flagged as part of an investigation. But individual agencies can choose to retain data for much longer.Flock's founder and CEO Garrett Langley told the BBC that it was up to individual cities to decide how long to store data and what information to share with whom."I don't think a technology company should be making decisions like that," he says."As long as it's a lawful investigation, we are not going to tell cities what laws they should or should not enforce."Flock is a safety, not surveillance, company, Langley says. Yet three patents filed between 2020 and 2025 have the word "surveillance" in the title.He boasts that the tech helped solve "about a million crimes" and helped find more than 10,000 missing people. "The debate of how we build a society where safety and privacy coexist" is worth having, he says, but the ongoing vandalism is "disappointing".But there is nothing Flock or law enforcement could say to make Jessie feel at ease with this technology, she says. "I just don't trust that they're doing it to keep us safe."

schema.headline: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?

title: Trump envoys arrive in Moscow ahead of Ukraine talks
description: The two envoys have travelled to Moscow on multiple occasions since Trump returned to office, but Sunday would be their first visit to Kyiv. Delegatio
body: The two envoys have travelled to Moscow on multiple occasions since Trump returned to office, but Sunday would be their first visit to Kyiv. Delegations from Ukraine have attended talks in the US over the past 18 months.Zelensky said on Saturday that Russia had fired "demonstrative" strikes on airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight ahead of his planned meeting with the US.Ukraine's president added: "Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport."Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.Zelensky said on Friday he would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace during the envoys' visit and called for Russia to do the same for Ukraine.He also said an overnight Russian strike on a civilian building in the Dnipro region killed four people and injured five others.Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Moscow comes just over a week after a rare visit to the Russian capital by the head of the CIA, John Ratcliffe. There was no official comment from Washington or the Kremlin on what was discussed. Speaking last week, Trump described the meeting as "semi-routine".Last year, the US, Ukraine and Russia separately suggested that a deal to end the war was edging closer following a flurry of talks brokered by the Americans. European allies also held talks in Paris but discussions ultimately ended without a breakthrough. Key disagreements remain between the warring sides on issues such as territory and security guarantees for Ukraine. In recent months, both Russia and Ukraine have intensified their aerial attacks as fighting continues.Ukraine said it has struggled to repel attacks due to a lack of interceptor missiles, while Kyiv has focused its strikes on Russian economic infrastructure targets.

schema.headline: Trump envoys arrive in Moscow ahead of Ukraine talks

title: Virgin's Richard Branson: Flight price rises due to 'foolish leaders' starting wars
description: Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson has blamed flight price rises on "foolish leaders" starting wars, in a thinly veiled reference to the US-Isra
body: Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson has blamed flight price rises on "foolish leaders" starting wars, in a thinly veiled reference to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.Middle East tensions have choked the production and transportation of millions of barrels of oil, causing a surge in the price of car and jet fuels, which are made from oil.In May, Virgin Atlantic added a fuel surcharge to ticket prices in response.US President Donald Trump has repeatedly defended the conflict as necessary for peace and security long-term.However, Sir Richard said there was "no need" for the war. "The Iran conflict was completely unnecessary. There was a nuclear agreement between Iran and the rest of the world that had been negotiated by President Obama and a lot of European people."It was working, so there was no need to rip it up... And this war has just resulted in much higher oil prices all over the world. And inflation has been one of the consequences."The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.The European benchmark jet fuel price had been hovering around $800 (£590) a tonne but spiked following the outbreak of the Iran war, reaching a peak of over $1,800 in April. It has since dropped to around $1,450. Virgin Atlantic's chief executive, Corneel Koster, told the BBC that for "this level of fuel price" fuel surcharges were "absolutely required", adding that it's "hard to be optimistic at this moment about the situation in the Middle East".The surcharge Virgin introduced added £50 to an economy class fare, £180 to premium and £360 to business class.

schema.headline: Virgin's Richard Branson: Flight price rises due to 'foolish leaders' starting wars

title: The Grand Tour's new presenters: 'I hope we prove the critics wrong'
description: For more than two decades, Top Gear and The Grand Tour were defined as much by the three men presenting them as by the cars they drove.Jeremy Clarkson
body: For more than two decades, Top Gear and The Grand Tour were defined as much by the three men presenting them as by the cars they drove.Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May built one of television's most recognisable partnerships, meaning anyone taking over The Grand Tour was always going to face a daunting task.Now YouTubers James Engelsman and Thomas Holland and, perhaps most unexpectedly, train enthusiast-turned-internet star Francis Bourgeois are stepping into their shoes for the new series.And, with initial reviews generally mixed, they knew they had some convincing to do."They literally changed the car world," Holland says of the previous trio.He understands why some fans have questions about whether the show should continue with anyone else."They're completely justified to feel that, because they did the same thing that we did - which is grow up watching Clarkson, Hammond and May."The show was a very important part of our lives as car enthusiasts."For a show built around the chemistry of its three former presenters, finding a replacement trio with such chemistry was always going to be as important as finding people who knew about cars.Engelsman and Holland are an already established double act as the presenters of Throttle House, a motoring YouTube channel with more than three million subscribers.The bigger unknown was who would become their third presenter.That search eventually led the show's producers to Francis Bourgeois, a social media star better known for standing on railway platforms than behind the wheel of a supercar.Engelsman says he and Holland had done chemistry testing with a number of people, but Bourgeois immediately felt different."As soon as Francis showed up, we were like: 'That guy'," Holland says.Bourgeois remembers their first meeting taking place on a leather sofa in a hotel outside Basingstoke, where they mostly talked about what cars they owned.By the time filming began, Holland says there was no need to consciously work out how to make the three-person dynamic function as "it just worked and clicked immediately".While the chemistry came quickly, actually finding out they had the job was much less straightforward. Engelsman says there was "no immediate moment" when they were formally told they had been chosen."It was the most gradual thing," he says.He and Holland initially thought they were simply part of a wider audition process, but then found themselves repeatedly being invited into writers' rooms and asked for their views on ideas for the show.For Bourgeois, that uncertainty may have been helpful as he admits he'd "just fall apart and start crying" if he'd found out about the job.There is a clear generational shift with the new presenters, all three of whom built their profiles on social media - and critics have been mixed on how successfully that translates to The Grand Tour. The Independent's three-star review, external described the reboot as "all rather safe" and said the presenters feel "stilted".The Guardian's review, external agreed and called the trio a "decent, if slightly anonymous, presence" who seem "quite meek and pleasant, and without any obvious dynamic".But it did praise Bourgeois, with Stuart Heritage calling him "the most enthusiastic enthusiast currently working on planet Earth".The FT also awarded the show three-stars, external and said that while the big budget spectacles are enjoyable to watch, they also feel "a little muted".It added that "the real question is whether a series that has been driven by big personalities like Clarkson, May and Hammond can survive with a new team".Bourgeois may be best known for his ecstatic trainspotting videos but he says his love of cars goes back just as far.Growing up near Willesden Junction in London, there were plenty of trains to watch, but he was also fascinated by the cars outside his home."There was a particular Mitsubishi Legnum VR-4 that was outside my parents' flat window and I just loved it," he tells me. "I suppose with my social media, I'm just showing one of my passions and I have really wanted to let out that car enthusiasm too."It's nice that these two sides of my very strong passions are in harmony together and it's been a real pleasure to drive some of the cars on The Grand Tour."His enthusiasm for transport more generally has already rubbed off on his co-presenters who say they've become "very educated by Francis on many things during long walks and long drives".

schema.headline: The Grand Tour's new presenters: 'I hope we prove the critics wrong'

title: Germany's far-right AfD bids for first taste of power in eastern vote
description: Germany is holding its breath this weekend as there is a seismic election in the country's east.The Alternative für Deutschland party is aiming to sec
body: Germany is holding its breath this weekend as there is a seismic election in the country's east.The Alternative für Deutschland party is aiming to secure a majority in the regional parliament of Saxony-Anhalt.An outright win would mark the first time a far-right party has held state-level power in the nation's post-war era.For the AfD's opponents, this is a point of serious peril. But the party sees it as a stepping stone towards its dreams of nationwide power.This is an election that could change German history.The result could also spell fresh trouble for embattled conservative (CDU) Chancellor Friedrich Merz, as rumours persist about whether he can see out his term in office.Booed during recent public appearances, Merz is hardly seen as an electoral asset.Perhaps the chancellor regrets a pledge to halt the rise of the far right, given that the exact opposite has happened.By contrast, the charismatic AfD lead candidate in the state - Ulrich Siegmund - appears to have enjoyed dominating discussion and media coverage.Dubbed "Germany's Most Dangerous Man" by Der Spiegel magazine, he has brushed off reports that people previously in the neo-Nazi scene are among those to hold influential roles around him.The 35-year-old can often be seen, including in his own many social media posts, amongst adoring crowds or happily riding a retro East German scooter.A lingering nostalgia for the past, alongside an acute dissatisfaction with the present, has fed the party's popularity in its eastern strongholds.Voters voice frustration with immigration, public safety, Germany's struggling economy, high energy costs and aid being sent abroad to countries like Ukraine.The party wants to segregate child refugees into special classes: "The refugee children should be given the message that their stay in Germany is only temporary."The manifesto claims that "sexual deviations and non-reproductive lifestyles" have been aggressively promoted over "normal family" structures.LGBT rainbow flags should be banned from being flown at schools, the party argues, while children should be taught less about the Nazis and more about positive aspects of German history.On immigration, a task-force would be set up as part of plans to detain and deport migrants who no longer have the right to be in the state, while the party also calls for an end to "illegal, culturally alien" mass migration.The AfD's pro-Russia sympathies have also sparked claims that it cannot be trusted with sensitive intelligence. When a Russian army mug was spotted in the office of leading AfD figure Hans-Thomas Tillschneider in Saxony-Anhalt, he said it was just a souvenir, and "it's not our war".That was as Berlin, this week, publicly blamed Moscow for a failed drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. The Kremlin has denied involvement.Meanwhile, German security sources have warned that Russian-backed disinformation campaigns, often against AfD rivals, have been escalating - something Moscow's representatives describe as "anti-Russian hysteria". State-level governments hold significant powers over areas including local education, policing and culture, while their delegates sit in the federal government's second chamber – the Bundesrat.An AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt would be able to implement changes locally and gain a louder voice on the national stage.The party remains strongest in the former communist east Germany but it is also leading the polls nationwide.That is despite warnings that it has morphed from a Eurosceptic party, founded in 2013, into one that flirts with, or attracts, extremist support.At one AfD rally, we saw a man wearing a T-shirt that read Arisch - the German word for Aryan that the Nazis used to promote their false theories of a master race.We do not know whether the man was a party supporter, a member or merely an attendee. He would not talk to us.Saxony-Anhalt is one of several states where the party is officially classed as right-wing extremist.Domestic intelligence charges the local branch with being infused by a "racist ideology" and anti-constitutional aims.The AfD, which says it is a conservative, libertarian movement, dismisses these designations as politicised smears and rejects any comparisons with National Socialism. Ulrich Siegmund has not ruled out getting rid of domestic intelligence (BfV) in the state if the AfD wins a majority.Other parties won't go into coalition with the AfD, as part of what is known as the Brandmauer or firewall that keeps the far right from government.That is why it must seek a parliamentary majority in order to be sure of securing power.In Saxony-Anhalt, it is no longer about creating cracks in the firewall but rather trying to bypass it altogether.Pulling that off will likely depend on whether other, smaller parties get enough votes in order to pass a 5% threshold that allows them to enter parliament.Politics is maths and Germany is no different, even if the maths can be quite convoluted.But if the AfD does score a decisive victory, then a party that uses anti-establishment rhetoric to grow its support will face a test it has never faced before.Grievances could still be laid at the door of the federal government in Berlin, but the AfD would no longer solely be able to rail against those in office because it would be in office itself.Saxony-Anhalt may be a relatively small state, by population, but it is about to host one hell of an election.

schema.headline: Germany's far-right AfD bids for first taste of power in eastern vote

title: Thieves steal 70,000 pints of Guinness in two lorries
description: Thieves have stolen more than 800 barrels of Guinness by driving off from a depot with two HGV trailers. About 70,000 pints worth of the stout, estima
body: Thieves have stolen more than 800 barrels of Guinness by driving off from a depot with two HGV trailers. About 70,000 pints worth of the stout, estimated to be worth £115,000, were taken from Whitehouse Industrial Estate on Aston Lane in Runcorn on Monday, Cheshire Police said.One wagon-load was taken at about 19:45 BST and a second one was stolen at about 21:30.  The stolen barrels - which each would hold about 88 pints - had been destined for pubs, the force added. Det Sgt McClatchy said: "It is famously said that 'Guinness is good for you', but that is only the case when it has been bought and paid for."

schema.headline: Thieves steal 70,000 pints of Guinness in two lorries

title: Diamond League results: Amy Hunt continues strong season with third in Diamond League final
description: Amy Hunt's strong late-season form showed no signs of letting up as she clocked a season's best 22.16 seconds, just eight hundredths off her lifetime
body: Amy Hunt's strong late-season form showed no signs of letting up as she clocked a season's best 22.16 seconds, just eight hundredths off her lifetime best, to finish third in 200m at the Diamond League final in Brussels.The Briton, who picked up four gold medals at the European Championships in Birmingham last month, was beaten by St Lucia's Julien Alfred, the fastest woman over the distance this year, who took victory in 21.79, and American Kayla White in 22.00."I'm really really proud of that one," Hunt told BBC World Service."That was probably one of the best bends I've ever done, if not the best. I could feel I was so close to Julian, then the long season kind of caught out to me in the last 20 metres."A third-place finish continues Hunt's upward trajectory in the finale of the 15-stop elite circuit.She came fifth and sixth respectively in the 2025 and 2024 Diamond League finals over 200m.Hunt will also run in the 100m event on Saturday night, drawn alongside American Olympic silver medallist Sha'Carri Richardson, and intends to similarly double up at the inaugural Ultimate Championships event in Budapest, which begin on 11 September."We train over 400 metres and the longest recovery we have in winter sessions is 45 seconds," added Hunt."I'm out there doing the really long reps back to back to back and that's enabling me to do this really packed schedule."Hunt finished furthest up the results list of any of the Britons in action.Matt Hudson-Smith was fifth in the 400m, well off Botswana's world champion Collen Kebinatshipi, while Jake Hayward, running in his Wales vest, was eighth in a captivating 1500m race.Australian 20-year-old Cameron Myers expertly picked a path to victory, edging out Kenyan teenager Phanuel Koech. Their rivalry could play out over plenty more big stages in the future.Elsewhere, world champion Oblique Seville took the 100m in 9.90 seconds and Kenya's Emmanuel Wanyonyi won his fourth successive Diamond League title over 800m.After Sweden's Armand 'Mondo' Duplantis opted not to compete in the pole vault final after feeling tightness in his leg, his Greek rival Emmanouil Karalis, who has climbed to second in the event's all-time list this year, took centre stage and victory with a 6.12m clearance.While Duplantis is a doubt for the all-star Ultimate Championships event, one of its biggest names will definitely be missing from the startlists after Olympic 100m champion Noah Lyles announced an injury-enforced early end to his season.

schema.headline: Diamond League results: Amy Hunt continues strong season with third in Diamond League final

title: Viral Chicken Shop Date moments that created a YouTube star
description: Recipe for success - the Chicken Shop Date moments that created a YouTube starImage source, Dimz IncImage caption, After more than 10 years, Amelia Di
body: Recipe for success - the Chicken Shop Date moments that created a YouTube starImage source, Dimz IncImage caption, After more than 10 years, Amelia Dimoldenberg announced Chicken Shop Date was shutting up shopByRiyah CollinsBBC Newsbeat and Tom RichardsonWhen someone says "we need to talk", it often means one thing - it's time to break up. After Amelia Dimoldenberg announced on Thursday her hit YouTube series Chicken Shop Date would be turning off the fryers after one last series, some fans were begging for a second chance, while others agreed it was time to move on. Over more than 10 years and 100 dates, Dimoldenberg's awkward flirting, deadpan silences and willingness to overshare has made her channel an unmissable stop for any celeb, single or not. Before one last slurp on an orange soda, BBC Newsbeat looks back at some of the talk show's most iconic moments. 'If someone says chicken girl, do you turn around?'Image source, Dimz IncImage caption, Daniel Kaluuya later went on to win an Oscar and was one of Dimoldenberg's breakthrough guestsChicken Shop Date grew out of a youth club project and interviews Dimoldenberg conducted with south London grime artists as a teenager for The Cut. She's spoken about how hard she had to work in the early days to persuade guests to come on the channel. Nearly five years into her series, in 2020, she bagged her first big name outside the rap scene: Oscar-nominated actor Daniel Kaluuya. During the date, Dimoldenberg admitted she would turn around when fans shouted "chicken" at her in the street.This YouTube post cannot be displayed in your browser. Please enable Javascript or try a different browser.View original content on YouTubeThe BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. YouTube content may contain adverts.Her interview with the Get Out star pulled in five million views - a fraction of the audience she'd go on to attract, but evidence her hard work was clearly starting to pay off.It laid the foundations for even bigger names to join Dimoldenberg, with Sir Paul McCartney, Lando Norris and Shania Twain among those placing orders.  'What's your name again?'Image source, Dimz IncImage caption, "Did you just call me Phoebe?" became one of the show's most viral moments Forgetting your date's name can be a guarantee that there won't be a second one. But in Dimoldenberg's case it created one of Chicken Shop Date's most memorable moments.During a 2023 date, she discussed marriage proposals with Jennifer Lawrence.When Dimoldenberg said she wouldn't know how it felt to be engaged, the Hunger Games star looked the host in the eye, and began:"Phoebe.""Did you just call me Phoebe?" Dimoldenberg responded."Yeah.""Amelia."The pair burst out laughing, but it wasn't the only time her date was caught thinking about someone else.  Pop star Sabrina Carpenter, who appeared on Chicken Shop Date in 2024, didn't forget the host's name, but did confuse the show with Hot Ones - the YouTube series where celebrities eat progressively spicy chicken wings.In a sign of her own rising stardom, Dimoldenberg took on the chilli challenge in the same year.'It's been vibey'Image source, Dimz IncImage caption, Fans were convinced by the on-screen chemistry between Dimoldenberg and Andrew Garfield The spice in this series was reserved for the guests - some more than others.After a couple of red carpet run-ins where there seemed to be palpable chemistry, actor Andrew Garfield's appearance on Dimoldenberg's show set the internet alight with speculation of genuine romance. When he appeared on Chicken Shop Date, Garfield conceded it had been "vibey" between them for a while, although for some viewers the encounter didn't live up to expectations.The following year, Dimoldenberg insisted the pair were just friends. Garfield wasn't the only guest to seem to really hit it off with the host. Singer Billie Eilish was especially flirty, giggling after complimenting Dimoldenberg's body. And after rapper Aitch came on the channel, rumours circulated it had kindled a real-life relationship, although neither ever confirmed this. Dates that jiggle jiggleImage source, Dimz IncImage caption, Dimoldenberg has collaborated with documentary maker Theroux multiple times since their dateIt was the clash of two interviewing titans - the master of the strategic pause and the queen of the awkward silence.But when Louis Theroux met Dimoldenberg the big takeaway wasn't a new, personal revelation. It was a viral rap.During the pair's 2022 date, the Chicken Shop Date host reminded the documentary maker of the time he spat some bars on his BBC series Weird Weekends, when his quest to become "the first white, middle-class gangsta rapper" took him to New Orleans in the US.This YouTube post cannot be displayed in your browser. Please enable Javascript or try a different browser.View original content on YouTubeThe BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. YouTube content may contain adverts.Despite the 20-year gap, Theroux was able to recall an impressive amount of Jiggle Jiggle, his rap about his love of red wine and the struggles facing the very tall owner of a compact car.Music producers Duke & Jones added autotune to a TikTok clip of the moment, turning it into a viral sensation that's had almost 84 million views since it was uploaded. Theroux eventually teamed up with the duo to record a new version of the song.So, a second date?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Amelia Dimoldenberg has been the host of Chicken Shop Date since 2014Unlucky in love Dimoldenberg hasn't had much success when it comes to second dates - but that doesn't stop her asking. She's been turned down by artists from Central Cee and Digga D to Rosalía."When I was 17, I thought that I might meet the love of my life on a date in a chicken shop," she wrote in her farewell statement. "Since then, I've spent my entire twenties sat across from the most incredible people, people I'd always dreamt of meeting. "All of them charmed me (some more than others), and I definitely charmed them."With one final series in the pipeline, there's still hope for some rekindled connections. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Viral Chicken Shop Date moments that created a YouTube star

title: Jay-Z: Stars join US rapper at long-awaited UK show
description: Jay-Z also took a moment to thank his fans who have been there from the beginning, telling them that "music saved my life". His reflective mood contin
body: Jay-Z also took a moment to thank his fans who have been there from the beginning, telling them that "music saved my life". His reflective mood continued as he performed Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem) and Where I'm From, which explores his upbringing in the Marcy housing projects in Brooklyn, New York.He cranked the energy back up for his 2011 hit No Church in the Wild, which was amplified by firey pyrotechnics that radiated heat through the stadium.Originally a collaboration with controversial rapper Ye, also known as Kanye West, Jay-Z left his voice in for the chorus but cut his verses out. US DJ Khaled had a brief moment on stage while Jay-Z changed, but it was the appearance of London-born rapper Giggs which got the crowd erupting. He appeared overwhelmed at one stage, his hand clutching his face, as he took in the packed crowd while performing his track Talkin Da Hardest alongside Jay-Z. The surprise guests didn't stop there, as Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean from the 90s American hip-hop collective Fugees reunited to perform their hit tracks Ready or Not, Killing Me Softly With His Song and Fu-Gee-La.It was a full circle moment for both them and Jay-Z as he recalled supporting them on their European tour. The US rap superstar closed out the night with rousing renditions of Public Service Announcement (Interlude) and Numb/Encore, hailing it as a "legendary night" that he would "never forget". The crowd appeared to agree as thousands praised him by holding up his famous diamond hand gesture.Fans had travelled from across the UK and the world to see the rapper, including Prince Dean Sithole, who hailed Jay-Z as one of his role models."I think he's very impacting, especially for us black people because we don't get a lot of recognition," the 19-year-old from Leeds told BBC Newsbeat."Seeing him today shows that dreams are possible and you can be that person that you want to be."Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, broke through with his 1996 debut album, but it was his third record, Vol. 2: Hard Knock Life, in 1998 which landed him the top spot in the US charts for the first time and a best rap album Grammy.He went on to establish himself as one of the most influential figures in hip-hop, releasing 13 solo studio albums and several collaboration records, which have secured him 25 Grammy Awards.He was also the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017, as well being inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.Over the years, he has also become one of the most prominent music mogul's in the world, with his company Roc Nation representing a host of top talent and, in recent years, it has been behind the Super Bowl half-time show.In 2019, he was declared hip-hop's first billionaire by Forbes, having built an empire based on music, property, fashion and investments alongside his wife Beyoncé.The power couple have three children, daughter Blue Ivy, 14, and 9-year-old twins, Rumi and Sir.

schema.headline: Jay-Z: Stars join US rapper at long-awaited UK show

title: Everton: David Moyes says he has never spoken to owner Dan Friedkin
description: David Moyes says he has never met or spoken to Everton owner Dan Friedkin since returning as manager in January 2025.Friedkin is head of The Friedkin
body: David Moyes says he has never met or spoken to Everton owner Dan Friedkin since returning as manager in January 2025.Friedkin is head of The Friedkin Group, which runs the club from its base in Houston, but has not attended a home game since completing a takeover of the club in December 2024.How the club is run and who is responsible for making key decisions came under close scrutiny during the summer transfer window.Speaking to reporters before Everton's match against Manchester United on Sunday, Moyes reiterated his commitment to the club despite a chaotic end to the window. When asked if he had ever met or spoken to Friedkin in the 20 months since he was reappointed as manager, Moyes' answer was a simple "No".Friedkin leaves the day-to-day running of the club to his son-in-law Rishi Majithia, who works in tandem with chief executive Angus Kinnear. "My real contact is Angus," said Moyes. "Angus is the one who I would go to see. Rishi is the next one and then the head of the Friedkin family in America."I don't really get any direct conversations with them, but I do through Rishi, he is the one I would speak to."Fans reacted angrily during last Saturday's match at Bournemouth following news the club had accepted a £40m bid from Nottingham Forest for one of their prized assets, England Under-19s midfielder Harrison Armstrong. Everton eventually pulled out of the deal, but supporters remain frustrated by decisions made by the board in the remainder of the transfer window. Beto was sold to Fiorentina on deadline day on Tuesday, before the club had secured a replacement striker, with USA forward Folarin Balogun then backing out of a move to Everton from Monaco at the 11th hour on Tuesday. Everton finished the transfer window with a squad of just 18 senior players, including only one striker, one right-back and one left-back.Moyes aligned himself with Everton fans last weekend when asked about plans to sell Armstrong, saying the club was "managed by an Evertonian" and "supporters aren't always wrong".And he acknowledged on Friday that there was work to do done on the club's structure behind the scenes: "We've got new owners in who are still feeling their way in the club. I think if we get to know each other more it will get better."But the former Manchester United and West Ham boss said he would not walk away from the challenge of unifying a club that he led to a succession of top-five finishes in the Premier League between 2002 and 2013 in his first stint as manager. "Everton's different," said Moyes, when asked if he had considered quitting. "I wouldn't have come back for anybody but Everton. "I think the club here has had enough days where the people find a way of recovering. People saw the face of Evertonians last week and it can be really powerful. I would expect them to be really powerful now."But powerful for the team, powerful for the players. What we're going to need from them is extra because we're short, so we need them. If they're not with us, then it's terrible. And they are with us, I believe they are with us."

schema.headline: Everton: David Moyes says he has never spoken to owner Dan Friedkin

title: Michael Owen doesn't tell his children he loves them - how big a deal is that?
description: Dad Aaron Dale, host of the Raisingboys2men podcast and author of a book on parenting, agrees."It's not words or actions - they shouldn't compete agai
body: Dad Aaron Dale, host of the Raisingboys2men podcast and author of a book on parenting, agrees."It's not words or actions - they shouldn't compete against each other, they should complement each other."Words are to speak the message and actions are the evidence."Dale pointed to how his own father would often tell him "I love you" after letting him down, diminishing the meaning of the words. However, some parents believe it is absolutely crucial their child hears that they are loved. One father of a seven-year-old daughter, told us he was surprised by Owen's comments, describing them as "awful". "You should always tell your children you love them no matter what, when they're bad, when they're good," he said. And reacting online to the clip of Owen, another parent wrote: "Parents and potential parents do not listen to this man. Tell your kids you love them everyday, even when it annoys them."To the outside observer, Owen's love for his children is not in doubt.The trailer for his new show, Meet the Owens, shows glimpses of what appears to be a happy home life with his wife and children. And in 2024, the former England striker spoke movingly about his son James's sight loss, saying: "If I could give him my eyes... I would."Pushed by podcast host Laing to explain why he doesn't let the 'I love yous' flow freely, Owen told Laing that "I would love to be a little bit soft"."I'm definitely getting softer," he said, "but still not soft enough to say anything like that."Using the word "soft" to describe telling your children you love them reflects long-standing attitudes many fathers have towards parenting, both Dale and Dr Britto suggest. They say it's a result of different contexts, such as culture, class, gender and a generational divide"I think that's the dangerous part there," Dale says, "the belief of what men should and what men shouldn't do."Many fathers believe their role is simply to "provide", but they can do so much more, he says. "Men are much more than just providers... what about our emotional capacity and willingness to have conversations and be there as fathers? And maybe we can't provide, but you know what? Our presence is at full capacity." He adds that he thinks people's style of parenting "always stems from somewhere", including whether they were often told they were loved as a child.Gender expectations and masculinity are not the only element at play, Dr Britto says."In some cultures they don't even use those words [I love you] at all," she says. "They may ask things like 'Have you eaten?' as a sign of love rather than actually saying 'I love you'."She adds: "As an African myself, in Nigerian culture parents don't always say 'I love you'... but I still felt loved."Parents also suggest that different generations may approach showing love for their children in different ways. Reacting on social media, one says Owen is right to suggest actions speak louder than words: "My dad never said the words, but it was also never in doubt."Another writes: "What's the big deal? My dad - and I'm sure most dads of our generation - didn't. He did something far, far better than emotional words he 'showed us' by his actions."While Owen's comments may have triggered strong feelings, it is clear there are countless ways parents communicate love to their children.Above all, says Dr Britto, it's about making sure children feel a sense of belonging. "Do they feel loved?" she says. "Do they feel wanted? "Do they feel that they matter, rather than simply hearing the words?"

schema.headline: Michael Owen doesn't tell his children he loves them - how big a deal is that?
